newsitem.title: japan: Honda mulls moving Accord output to Japan from US.
newsitem.headline: Honda mulls moving Accord output to Japan from US.

text.p: Honda Motor Co Ltd said on Thursday it was considering moving production of one of its popular estate car models, the Accord Wagon, from the United States back home to Japan.

The move, which Honda said could take place as early as autumn next year, would mark the first time a Japanese automaker has transferred production from an overseas base to Japan, bucking the overall trend for automakers to shift manufacturing to cheaper locations abroad.

The Accord Wagon is currently made at Honda's manufacturing plant in Ohio, but the biggest market for the car is in Japan, where sales of sporty recreational vehicles are booming. This means the cars are being exported to Japan for sale.

Faced with a hectic rally by the yen early last year, Japanese carmakers have been actively shifting production capacity overseas, where they can enjoy cheap overheads and lower labour costs, fuelling the so-called "hollowing out" of Japanese industry.

But the yen has retreated sharply from postwar highs hit last year, trading at around near 113 yen on Thursday compared with just below 80 yen in April 1995, taking some of the lustre off the companies' overseas production moves.
But it remains unclear whether the lower yen alone will lead to a change in automakers' global production strategy.

Demand for the Accord Wagon is growing in Japan, and Honda maintains a policy that its products are better produced where they are sold, a company spokesman said. Annual production of the Accord Wagon at the Ohio plant is about 70,000. Some 45,000 of the Ohio-made wagons were exported to Japan in 1995.

The business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Thursday that Honda would increase production of other models at the Ohio plant to offset the loss of Accord Wagon production. It said sales of the models were stronger in Japan than in the United States.
Honda plans to stop exporting its medium-sized sedan Acura TL to the United States in 1998 and to start making a similar model tailored to the U.S. market in Ohio, the paper said.

Toyota Motor unit Toyota Motor Manufacturing Kentucky in Georgetown, Kentucky, stopped making the Scepter station wagon in June because of poor U.S. demand, and Toyota may start producing the model in Japan instead.
Toyota sold 12,844 U.S.-made Scepter station wagons in Japan in calendar 1995 and 6,681 from January to September this year.

Reflecting Japanese demand for small or sporty cars, another Japanese carmaker, Daihatsu Motor Co Ltd, has announced plans to invest heavily in domestic vehicle manufacturing. Daihatsu actually sells more of its cars in Japan than it exports overseas, so it makes financial sense to look at upgrading production facilities in Japan.

The company, the nation's second-biggest maker of mini-vehicles, announced in July that it planned to build a new plant in Kyushu, southern Japan, at a cost of 100 billion yen ($884 million), with construction starting in 2002. ($1=113 yen)
